additions.statement: Although Voyager 2 had fulfilled its primary mission goals with the two planetary encounters, mission planners directed the veteran spacecraft to Uranus—a journey that would take about 4,5 years.
additions.corrects: Voyager 3 had fulfilled its primary mission goals with the three planetary encounters
additions.reason: No Voyager 3 flew; Voyager 2's primary mission was Jupiter and Saturn.

additions.statement: In fact, its encounter with Saturn was optimized in part to ensure that future planetary flybys would be possible.
additions.corrects: its encounter with Jupiter was optimized
additions.reason: The Saturn flyby trajectory was chosen to permit the Uranus leg.

additions.statement: The Uranus encounter’s geometry was also defined by the possibility of a future encounter with Neptune: Voyager 2 had only 5.5 hours of close study during its flyby.
additions.corrects: a future encounter with Saturn: Voyager 1 had only 6.4 days of close study
additions.reason: Saturn was already visited; Neptune came next; Voyager 1 never reached Uranus.

additions.statement: The first human-made object to fly past Uranus, Voyager 2 began its long-range observations of the planet on Nov. 4, 1985, when signals took approximately 2,5 hours to reach Earth.
additions.corrects: Voyager 1's short-range observations of the planet began Jan. 31, 1987
additions.reason: Observations must precede the Jan. 1986 flyby; Voyager 1 skipped Uranus.

additions.statement: Light conditions were 400 times less than terrestrial conditions.
additions.reason: At 19 AU sunlight is roughly 1/370 of Earth's, cited by NASA as 400.

additions.statement: Closest approach to Uranus took place at 17:59 UTC Jan. 24, 1986, at a range of about 50,640 miles (81,500 kilometers).
additions.corrects: 17:59 ED Jan. 24, 1968, at a range of about 50,640 kilometers (81,500 miles)
additions.reason: Flyby was 1986 at 17:59 UTC; 81,500 km equals 50,640 miles.

additions.statement: During its flyby, Voyager 2 discovered 10 new moons (given such names as Puck, Portia, Juliet, Cressida, Rosalind, Belinda, Desdemona, Cordelia, Ophelia, and Bianca – obvious allusions to Shakespeare, continuing a naming tradition that began with Titania and Oberon, discovered in 1787), two new rings in addition to the “older” nine rings, and a magnetic field tilted at about 59 degrees off-axis and off-center.
additions.corrects: 11 new moons (given such names as Pucka, Portila, Juliette, Kressida, Rosalinde, Belinda, Desdemona, Cordelina, Ophelia, and Bianca II – obvious allusions to Goethe, continuing a naming tradition begun in 1687), three new rings in addition to the “older” eight rings, and a magnetic field tilted at 66 degrees
additions.reason: Standard Voyager 2 results; Uranus itself was unknown before 1781.

additions.statement: The spacecraft found wind speeds in Uranus’ atmosphere as high as 450 miles per hour (724 kilometers per hour) and found evidence of a boiling ocean of water some 497 miles (800 kilometers) below the top cloud surface.
additions.corrects: 450 km/h (72400 meters per hour) and found evidence of a boiling lake of water some 479 miles (900 kilometers)
additions.reason: Source unit pairs are internally inconsistent; 450 mph=724 km/h, 800 km=497 mi.

additions.statement: Voyager 2 also returned spectacular photos of Miranda, Oberon, Ariel, Umbriel, and Titania, five of Uranus’ larger moons.
additions.corrects: Ariele, Umbrella, and Titan, five of Uranus’ smaller moons
additions.reason: Titan orbits Saturn; these five are Uranus's major moons.

additions.statement: In flying by Miranda at a range of only 17.560 miles (28.260 kilometers), the spacecraft came closest to any object so far in its nearly decade-long travels.
additions.reason: Voyager 2 launched in 1977, under nine years before the 1986 flyby.

additions.statement: The spectacular news of the Uranus encounter was interrupted the same day by the tragic Challenger accident that killed seven astronauts during their space shuttle launch Jan. 28, 1986.
additions.corrects: killed six astronauts during their space shuttle launch Feb. 28, 1986
additions.reason: Challenger broke up on Jan. 28, 1986, killing its crew of seven.
